title: Cardinality Is a Design Decision
content:
Every high-cardinality incident I have worked through has the same origin story: someone needed a dimension, added a label, and the system got slower or more expensive over a period of weeks that nobody connected to the commit.
The reason labels are dangerous is not that they are expensive per se. It is that the natural intuition about them is inverted. In a database, adding a column is nearly free and you add columns freely. In a metrics system, adding a label multiplies the number of time series by the number of distinct values of that label, across every series that carries it. It is not a column. It is a cross product.
So the review question for any new label is not "is this useful" but "how many distinct values will this have, and what is the product when it is combined with the labels already on the metric". That is a conversation about a number, and it is the only kind that goes well, because both sides of it are arguing about something measurable.
The design habit I have ended up with: labels describe the shape of the metric, and high-cardinality or unbounded values belong somewhere else. Service, environment, and method are labels. User, request, build hash, and anything drawn from a path or an ID are not.
The interesting cases are the ones where you genuinely need the dimension. Per-tenant metrics, per-endpoint metrics with unbounded path segments. The answer there is not "do not do it", it is to put it in the right system. Traces handle per-request identity naturally. Logs handle high-cardinality fields naturally. A metrics system is built for aggregation, and per-request data in it is a category error that happens to be affordable until it is not.
The operational part is less interesting and more important. Cardinality limits that reject writes silently are worse than no limit, because your service is now lossy and nothing says so. And a per-metric series count, alarmed on a breakdown rather than a total, is what turns this from a quarterly surprise into a review conversation.
References Naming — the official best practices page, which warns about exactly this: every unique label combination is a new time series. High cardinality alerts — PromQL queries to find the offending metric, which is more useful than a theory about where it is. Grafana Mimir documentation — for when you are federating or running multi-tenant rather than a single Prometheus.
